archetype.name: Playoff Team (offense-led, pass-rush backed)
archetype.definition: A team with a top-10 offense when Caleb Williams plays, a defense that gets off the field on third down, and a record roughly backed by its efficiency, though not quite a contender's profile yet.

report.headline: Williams is back, the offense is humming, and the 6-2 record is mostly earned.
report.take:
Chicago in Ben Johnson's second year is an offense-first team that has finally added a defense worth mentioning. The offense ranks third in yards per game and ninth in pass EPA, and the Bears lead the league in time of possession. The record looks better than the numbers in a few places, and the reason is a quarterback carousel more than luck. Williams started the first two games, Case Keenum won two in his place, and Tyson Bagent's lone start was a 7-31 collapse at Green Bay with five giveaways. Since Williams returned, the offense has scored 31, 30 and 34, with positive passing EPA every week, including against Seattle's fifth-ranked defense.

The structural change from last year is on defense. The 2025 team won 11 games on borrowed luck: it led the league in turnover margin, outran its expected wins by 2.82, and ranked 21st in defensive EPA. This group gives up a lot less. It ranks first in third-down rate allowed, fourth in pressure rate and second in sack rate. Opponents rarely sustain drives, which is a big reason the offense owns the clock. The cost is the deep ball. The defense ranks last in EPA allowed on deep throws and 22nd in explosive pass rate, so it gives up long completions while taking away everything underneath.

The numbers point both ways. The turnover margin is 27th per game, which looks like a real flaw, but much of it comes from that one Bagent afternoon in Green Bay. With Williams under center the ball has mostly been safe. On the other side, the point differential implies 4.9 wins against six actual wins, and the Bears have covered every game they won. Some of the record is breaks. Net EPA ranks eighth, so this is a good team playing slightly above its level, not a fraud.

The second half will test that. The Bears trail Minnesota in a division where all four teams have winning records, and four of the final eight games are divisional. Detroit, Buffalo and Jacksonville also bring top-five offenses. That is where the deep-ball leak will cost them points. A flagged-up offensive line and a quarterback who holds the ball for over three seconds also invite sacks against good fronts.

strengths.title: Williams-led passing offense
strengths.body: The passing game ranks ninth in EPA and sixth in overall success rate, and it has driven three straight 30-point games since Williams returned. Williams gets time to work the full field, with the third-longest time to throw in the league. The receiving work is spread across Luther Burden III, Colston Loveland and Rome Odunze, so no single matchup shuts the offense down. It should hold as long as Williams stays healthy.

strengths.title: Third-down defense with real pressure
strengths.body: Chicago allows conversions on 26.1% of third downs, best in the league. The rush ranks fourth in pressure rate and second in sack rate, so offenses rarely finish drives. Pressure is one of the stickier defensive traits, and it travels better than takeaway luck.

strengths.title: Owning the clock and the margins
strengths.body: The Bears lead the league in time of possession and rank fifth in special-teams EPA per game. Together those shorten games, protect leads and hand the offense good field position. Ball control follows from the efficient offense and the third-down defense, so it should last.

concerns.title: Deep shots beat this secondary
concerns.body: The defense ranks last in EPA allowed on deep passes even though it ranks fourth against short throws. It takes away the underneath game but gets beaten over the top. With safety Coby Bryant on IR into December and corner Malik Muhammad II missing time, the problem has a personnel cause and is unlikely to fix itself. The Detroit, Buffalo and Jacksonville offenses ahead will test it.

concerns.title: Record slightly ahead of the play
concerns.body: The point differential implies fewer wins than the Bears have, and they rank eighth in wins over expected. Last year's 11-win team was much luckier, so this year's version is more legitimate. Still, expect the close-game breaks to even out somewhat against a back-loaded schedule.

concerns.title: Turnovers and line penalties
concerns.body: Chicago ranks 27th in turnover margin per game and 26th in offensive line penalties. The turnovers are mostly one five-giveaway game without Williams, so that part should improve. The line flags are spread across the season, including a 133-penalty-yard game at Atlanta, and they keep putting a long-holding passer behind the chains.

trend.note: The middle of the season had a backup-QB dip that bottomed out at Green Bay. Since Williams returned, the Bears have won three straight with 30-plus points, capped by a convincing 34-17 win in Seattle as underdogs.

nextGame.headline: Tampa's elite defense, broken offense: protect the ball and win.
nextGame.body:
Tampa Bay is a lopsided 3-5 team. Its defense ranks third in EPA allowed and second against the pass, while its offense ranks 28th and 30th in pass EPA. It is also better than its record: it has a positive point differential and has won only one of six one-score games. The Bucs' defense doesn't get home, though, ranking 30th in pressure rate. That suits a Williams offense that holds the ball and wins late in the down. Tampa smothers short throws and shuts down opposing WR1s, but it leaks to WR2s and is ordinary on deep balls. Its offense will try to run and shorten the game, and it has a line ranked 28th in sack rate facing Chicago's second-ranked sack defense. The Book has Chicago -6 with a 46.5 total.

Availability favors Chicago on offense. Tampa is without WR Emeka Egbuka, an 86%-snap starter, and LB Yaya Diaby, with linebacker and corner depth also on IR. On Chicago's side, the defense's health matters most. CB Malik Muhammad II missed Seattle with a toe injury, and DE Grady Jarrett (groin) and DT Kentavius Street (knee) both left that game. All three carry return estimates for this week, but those are estimates. Missing Jarrett would dent the pass rush, and missing Muhammad would thin a secondary already without Coby Bryant. RB Kyle Monangai's thumb injury leaves more work for D'Andre Swift.

waysToWin.title: Clean pocket, patient Williams
waysToWin.body: Tampa's pass rush ranks 30th in pressure rate, so Williams should get time to work the field. That clean pocket opens intermediate and deep throws instead of the short game the Bucs defend well. Without pressure, this elite coverage unit can be outlasted.

waysToWin.title: Attack away from the WR1
waysToWin.body: Tampa has held opposing WR1s furthest under their averages of any defense, but it ranks 29th against WR2s. Moving volume toward Rome Odunze and Colston Loveland, rather than forcing it to Burden, targets the soft spot in the coverage.

waysToWin.title: Rush wins against a leaky line
waysToWin.body: Tampa's passing offense is bottom-three in EPA, allows sacks at the 28th-ranked rate, and is now without Egbuka. If Chicago stops the run on early downs, its second-ranked sack rate takes over on third downs. Getting Tampa into obvious passing situations is the key.

waysToLose.title: Giving Tampa's ballhawks gifts
waysToLose.body: The Bucs rank fourth in takeaways, and Chicago's turnover margin is bottom-six. A low-scoring game against a top-three defense is exactly when one interception or fumble decides it. The Minnesota loss, a 3-9 game against the top defense, is the template to avoid.

waysToLose.title: Tampa runs it and shortens the game
waysToLose.body: Tampa is a run-heavy offense with an efficient ground game, ranked eighth in run EPA. Chicago's run defense is only mid-pack. If the Bucs stay on schedule, Chicago's pass rush never gets its passing downs and the game stays one-score into the fourth quarter.

waysToLose.title: Backs and tight ends underneath
waysToLose.body: Chicago's defense ranks 30th in EPA allowed to lead backs and 28th to TE1s. Tampa already sends more of its targets to running backs than the league norm, and with Egbuka out the ball will likely go there even more. That is the one area where a bad passing offense can move the chains on this defense.

nextGame.watch: Whether Williams gets clean third-down looks against Tampa's weak rush without turning the ball over to its top-four takeaway defense.

restOfSeason.body:
Chicago's offense should stay top-10 as long as Williams starts, and the third-down defense and pass rush have enough underlying strength to carry over. The turnover margin should improve now that the Bagent-start disaster is behind them. The win total should cool a little, because the record runs ahead of the point differential. The back half is also the hard part: two games with Detroit, trips to Buffalo and Minnesota, and visits from Jacksonville and Green Bay. Most of those opponents can attack the deep-ball hole.

The realistic path is a double-digit-win season and a playoff berth, probably as a wild card unless the Bears take the season finale in Minnesota. Points allowed will likely tick up against the high-powered offenses left on the schedule. A healthy Bryant in December would help.
swingFactors: Deep-pass defense vs. DET, BUF, JAX
Jarrett and the secondary getting healthy

confidence.note: Eight games across three starting QBs, with a hard back-half schedule.
